content.title: 12 000 large roofs can generate electricity: how do we turn potential into reality?
content.description: An untapped energy source lies on 12 000 Swedish roofs. Large properties can generate their own solar electricity, easing pressure on the electricity system by producing power where it is used. Why is solar power on large roofs expanding so slowly in Sweden compared with the rest of Europe?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's large roofs are among the country's most underestimated resources. Shopping centres, apartment buildings, warehouses and sports halls can become power plants that generate electricity exactly where it is needed, while making properties active participants in the electricity system.

The potential is enormous: 12 000 large roofs could generate substantial amounts of solar electricity. The European Commission's own analysis identifies self-consumed solar power as one of Europe's greatest untapped opportunities. Yet Sweden is falling behind. Alongside Estonia and Finland, we are one of the few EU countries with strict restrictions on those wishing to generate their own electricity.

Join a conversation between key players in solar energy, energy storage and property about what is needed to unlock this potential, and how new technology can enable properties to contribute more than ever to the electricity system.

content.title: From grassroots movement to personal brand – what happens to the collective 'we'?
content.description: Many civil society movements have grown out of shared commitment. Yet today, organisations often build their visibility on strong personal brands and well-known figures. What happens to the collective 'we' when movements increasingly revolve around individuals? Is it a gain or a loss?
content.extendedDescription:
Today there is a tension between grassroots engagement and personal branding.

Traditional popular movements are based on membership. They start from democratic structures and have a shared vision. Digital platform algorithms are designed the other way round. Faces and personal stories are favoured over the collective.
When the focus shifts to the personal brand (influencers, charismatic leaders), the movement risks becoming centred on one person. The 'we' is replaced by a vertical relationship between a 'star' and an audience. Engagement arises but is vulnerable. When the person falls, the cause often falls too.

Instead of co-creating a movement, we risk becoming consumers of someone's brand. Our role is to be 'followers', rather than a shared voice. But are 'personal brands' entirely bad?

How can a future balance be struck in which the 'we' is not weakened – and can actually be strengthened by personal 'brands'?
Has the balance already tipped, and if so, what is needed for the future?
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Together against cancer – when does prevention become a political responsibility?
content.description: Political decisions today can affect how many people develop cancer tomorrow. The European Code Against Cancer highlights 14 measures to reduce cancer risk, but it depends on political decisions and structural changes. How can Sweden reverse the trend as more people develop cancer?
content.extendedDescription:
While more people are living with cancer or have been treated for it, the number of new cases is increasing. A substantial proportion of cancer cases could be prevented through changes in lifestyles, the environment and societal structures. The European Code Against Cancer presents 14 recommendations to reduce and alleviate the burden of cancer – but several require political decisions and long-term investment in public health.

The seminar focuses on prevention and political responsibility. How can we reduce the number of new cases and give healthcare services better conditions for treating the cancers that do occur?

Among other topics, we discuss the cost of failing to invest in public health and cancer prevention, and the political decisions needed for Sweden to fulfil the European Code Against Cancer by shifting responsibility from individuals to society.

content.title: Electric aviation has taken off: what happens next?
content.description: Electrifying regional aviation opens the door to systemic change. Alongside fossil-free flights, smaller aircraft and lower operating costs enable a denser route network in Sweden. Locally generated electricity gives control over aviation's energy supply and increases resilience.
content.extendedDescription:
During the spring, 30 electric aircraft flights took place on Gotland as part of the NATO exercise Aurora 2026.

These flights offer hope for an island wholly dependent on functioning transport. They open new possibilities for sustainable access to Sweden's largest island and other parts of the country.

Electrifying regional aviation opens the door to broader systemic change. Besides enabling fossil-free flights, smaller aircraft and lower operating costs allow a denser Swedish route network. Locally generated electricity also gives control over aviation's energy source and contributes to a new level of resilience.

The seminar draws on lessons from the spring's electric demonstration flights. What is now needed to take the next step, from demonstrations to scheduled services in Sweden?

content.extendedDescription:
Electricity infrastructure faces a choice. The need for more capacity, robustness and rapid electrification is growing, while conventional grid expansion is often costly, slow and difficult to adapt to a more decentralised energy system. Lund is now developing EnergyNet, a new energy distribution architecture based on energy routers, open protocols and distributed control of electricity between buildings. Using the Pottugnen/Spjället pilot as a concrete example, we discuss how local meshed electricity networks can turn buildings into active nodes that produce, share, store and manage energy, taking the internet as a model.

Jonas Birgersson, "Bredbandsjesus", helped drive Sweden's internet transformation and now applies the same architectural thinking to electricity grids. Together with Dr. Marc Weiss, who helped shape Silicon Valley, we describe how EnergyNet could launch an Energy Valley in Skåne, with greater energy security, lower local energy costs, stronger robustness, growth and new skilled jobs.

content.title: Are problems always someone else's fault? Religion, migration and responsibility
content.description: Societies facing uncertainty and change can easily be tempted to blame ‘others’. How does this affect views of migration, religion and integration? This discussion explores how shared responsibility can build trust and cohesion in a pluralist Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
In his book Öppna era hjärtan, Simon Sorgenfrei places our culturally and religiously pluralist situation in the context of the past fifty years of Swedish history, particularly Muslim experiences in Sweden. He shows how religious expressions and experiences can shape people's identities, contributing to a more nuanced discussion of migration and encounters between religions.
This book discussion between Simon Sorgenfrei, Maha Alhaddad and Jan Eckerdal highlights religion's role in Sweden today, both as a source of conflict and as a resource and opportunity for greater trust and cohesion.
The conversation covers religious literacy, secularisation and what happens when religion is reduced to a private matter.
Musicians in Vårdklockans kyrka open and close the discussion. Refreshments are provided.

content.description: Sweden faces major skills challenges while many people remain far from the labour market. Labour market entry jobs are highlighted as an important reform for integration and skills supply — but why has their impact been limited so far, and what is needed next?

Labour market entry jobs are highlighted as an important reform to create more routes into a first job and strengthen integration, but their impact has so far been limited.

content.title: What happens if business gets to steer total defence planning?
content.description: Total defence involves everyone – not least business, which supplies most of the goods and services needed. But companies are often brought into total defence planning late. What happens if the perspective is reversed and companies' needs and solutions become the starting point instead?
content.extendedDescription:
The national adviser for stronger public-private cooperation in total defence is tasked with driving closer cooperation between the public sector and business. Could one approach be to reverse the perspective and start from companies' situations?

At the seminar, national adviser Charlotte Petri Gornitzka highlights several examples together with representatives of four companies:
- At the high-level Merkurius course, organised by the adviser together with ICA and others, companies' perspectives dominated the questions. What lessons were learned?
- Volvo does not wait for an invitation from the public sector, but invites others to total defence workshops centred on its own factories. What happens then?
- Tetra Pak actively participates in work to develop a standard for business preparedness. How can this work strengthen total defence?
- Heidelberg Materials produces cement – a potentially critical resource in wartime. How does the company view its role in Sweden's total defence?

content.title: The wave of reforms – a boost or a collapse in learning for Swedish schools?
content.description: The government is implementing extensive school reforms. Ambitions are high, but can Swedish schools manage so many changes at once, or could the most important thing of all suffer: pupils' learning?
content.extendedDescription:
The government is pushing through a reform package unprecedented in modern times: new grades, new curricula, new teacher training and a complete overhaul of the independent school system. Ambitions are high and some reforms are necessary. But can Swedish schools implement so many changes? Or will the most important thing of all suffer: pupils' learning?

Critics warn that some reforms risk dismantling successful schools, forcing school providers to close well-functioning operations and creating a system in which political enthusiasm takes precedence over educational reality. Others see an opportunity finally to address longstanding problems.

Are the reforms strengthening Swedish schools, or heading towards a loss of learning for an entire generation?

content.title: The school system fails the most vulnerable, but some independent schools make a difference. What makes the system dysfunctional?
content.description: Special education for pupils with mobility difficulties is lacking, limiting their physical and intellectual development. Schools are responsible for everyone's right to movement, yet habilitation services direct provision for this group. Why? People with mobility disabilities can develop and have a lifelong right to grow.
content.extendedDescription:
Part of Almega Utbildning's "Forum för svensk skola".

Sweden has special education approaches for deaf and blind people and those with intellectual disabilities, but not for people with mobility disabilities. Yet disability is almost always represented by a wheelchair. Consequently, thousands of children and young people with mobility disabilities:

• Encounter schools lacking knowledge of how motor limitations affect learning.
• Receive interventions directed by regional habilitation services rather than schools' educational remit.
• Must learn abstractly what others learn through their bodies.
• Fall into gaps between responsible organisations.

Independent schools can work more flexibly and individually. They often show greater ability to meet these pupils' needs. Yet there is still no nationally recognised pedagogy to draw on.

• Introductory presentation: a headteacher's perspective.
• Civil society voices: Neuroförbundet, RBU and Hjärnfonden participate.
• Political panel: reflection and dialogue on what the parties want to do.

content.title: A message to Sweden's next government: we are ready to win the battle for future investment
content.description: Competitiveness is determined not by ambition or strategy documents, but by where investment actually lands, where innovations scale and where industrial resilience is built.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is one of the world's most innovation-driven countries. We have strong private R&D, an active capital market and a world-class industrial base. content.title: How much truth can we handle? How do we recognise when a lie becomes the truth?
content.description: In politics, the same facts are used to reach different conclusions while disinformation and distrust spread. A crisis of truth emerges. Red lines are there not to be crossed, but when facts are ignored, they are crossed anyway. What happens to democracy, the state and its citizens when we become loose with the truth?
content.extendedDescription:
In a polarised debate, truth risks becoming a tool rather than common ground – but where is the line between interpretation and stretching the truth? What happens to democracy when we ourselves share uncertain information and contribute to this shift?

• How are crises of truth exposed, and how can we best counter disinformation, fake news, conspiracy theories and growing distrust of institutions that produce knowledge?
• What happens when people, who may already be in vulnerable situations, also lose confidence in public agencies and the institutions that underpin society?
• How can trust in society best be built over time?
• Where are our own 'red' lines in relation to what is happening?

The Christian tradition has a strong ideal of truth. 'The truth will set you free' (the Gospel of John). But what does that expression mean in a public debate where facts are interpreted, simplified and sometimes distorted? What is the difference between truth and interpretation? What responsibility do we all bear?
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: From vision to reality: how can electric aviation strengthen regional growth?
content.description: The electrification of aviation creates new opportunities for regional development. Smaller aircraft, lower operating costs and fossil-free operation open up new ways to organise air services and improve accessibility. How can the public and private sectors create the conditions for electric aviation?
content.extendedDescription:
In the project Elflyget som motor för regional tillväxt, tillgänglighet och hållbarhet, four Swedish regions have analysed how electric aviation can help develop the transport system of the future. The results show that the electrification of aviation is not just a technological innovation, but a broader systemic shift involving business models, infrastructure, energy systems and public governance.

A central question is how sustainable business models can be developed. Experience from public transport, regional mobility and public–private partnerships shows that new forms of collaboration can play a decisive role.

The seminar presents the project's findings and brings regions, airports, operators, developers and investors together to discuss the next steps. How can the public and private sectors jointly create the conditions for electric aviation to become part of future regional mobility?

content.title: Stable conditions for civil society funding – where are the political visions?
content.description: Civil society needs stable conditions for funding and giving. But there is no clear political vision for the long-term funding of non-profit organisations or a Swedish model for everyday philanthropy. How do politicians view sustainable funding for a strong, independent civil society?
content.extendedDescription:
Non-profit organisations create considerable value for society, from social support and international work to research, culture and activities for children and young people. To operate over the long term, they need stable, predictable funding conditions. Yet many organisations face financial uncertainty. Time-limited project funding and targeted grants from both public and private donors can restrict opportunities for long-term initiatives.

A strong civil society therefore needs a range of sustainable funding models and the ability to be an independent, sometimes uncomfortable voice in public debate. Before the 2022 election, neither tax relief on donations, public matching of donations nor simpler rules for corporate giving featured on the agenda of the parties behind the Tidö Agreement. However, interest has grown during this parliamentary term. How do the parties view civil society's future role and funding? We invite politicians to a discussion.

The seminar is part of Civilsamhällesarenan #Civsamarenan

content.title: How we make it harder for criminals to use Swedish ports and sea routes for smuggling
content.description: As much of Sweden is surrounded by water, many smuggling routes pass through maritime zones. How do we strengthen our joint efforts to prevent our sea routes and ports from becoming an arena for smuggling and organised crime?
content.extendedDescription:
Drug smuggling and sales are central to organised crime in Sweden, particularly among established criminal networks with significant capacity to pose threats. Sea routes and Swedish ports are one arena for this crime, while also being a lifeline for passenger and freight transport to and from Sweden. Several authorities have cooperated for many years through various checks in port areas, but a larger joint initiative against crime has been under way since last year. It involves stronger supervision and controls, better information sharing and legislative changes.

Join a highly topical seminar on how we can jointly intensify efforts to make it harder for criminals to use sea routes and ports for criminal activity — and help make Sweden safer.

content.title: Sweden's action against falsely flagged vessels and the so-called shadow fleet
content.description: How do we act against falsely flagged vessels and the so-called shadow fleet operating in our waters? What have we learned from this spring's boardings, and how do we proceed?
content.extendedDescription:
Since Russia began its war against Ukraine, the number of so-called shadow vessels has increased markedly in the Baltic Sea and along Sweden's coast. Recently, we have seen a new trend: more vessels sailing under false flags and with inadequate documentation. Vessels that disregard national and international law and choose to violate international agreements pose a high risk to shipping in Swedish waters, our shipping lanes and ports, and particularly the environment.

Kustbevakningen, working closely with other agencies, has therefore decided to intervene by boarding several vessels, after which their masters were remanded in custody and the vessels prohibited from use.

Welcome to a highly topical seminar on the strategy behind Sweden's actions.

content.title: How do we handle hybrid threats in our neighbouring maritime area?
content.description: Threats to underwater infrastructure, substandard ships, environmentally hazardous discharges, drone incidents, GPS interference… In recent years, a range of new threats has emerged against Swedish society and the maritime domain.
content.extendedDescription:
Hybrid threats can take different forms. At sea, we have seen several examples of damaged underwater infrastructure, and we regularly hear reports of navigation interference and drone incidents, information influence operations and cybersecurity threats. At the same time, we see ships in poor condition operated by unqualified crews, with no or limited insurance and under false flags. Extensive oil transport in the Baltic Sea and our neighbouring waters also poses an obvious risk of accidents and serious environmental damage. The difficulty of holding those responsible to account is itself a security risk.

Join a timely seminar about how we are working to strengthen resilience and act proactively against hybrid threats.

content.title: From genetic data to treatment: how do we build equitable cancer care nationwide?
content.description: Precision diagnostics shifts the focus from cancer's location in the body to the tumour's genetic profile. But advanced testing requires specialist expertise and structures for interpreting large datasets. How do we ensure equitable access to the right testing and treatment throughout the country?
content.extendedDescription:
A Molecular Tumour Board (MTB) is a central function in modern cancer care, where multidisciplinary expert teams interpret complex genetic information to select the right treatment for the right patient. But access to both advanced genetic testing and MTB expertise varies across the country. This risks reinforcing inequalities in cancer care and hindering implementation of precision medicine in clinical practice. How do we ensure every patient has access to the right diagnostics, interpretation and treatment, regardless of where they live?

The seminar focuses on the strategic choice facing Sweden:
• How do we make MTB a national concern adapted to regional needs?
• What investments are needed in infrastructure, expertise and data management?
• How do we ensure innovation translates into actual patient benefits for everyone, not just some?

The discussion brings together decision-makers, healthcare providers and experts to identify concrete ways forward.

content.title: Ukrainian veterans' perspectives – new knowledge for reintegration and societal development
content.description: Since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have served in the war. Veterans are a highly respected and influential group in society. How do their wartime experiences affect their views on key societal issues?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar draws on a new survey of Ukrainian veterans' attitudes to issues including democracy, gender equality, social inclusion and trust. The study is a collaboration between Försvarshögskolan and Folke Bernadotteakademin. The results show that differences between veterans and civilians are often smaller than expected, but that specific experiences – particularly war injuries and the transition to civilian life – are especially significant in shaping attitudes.
The seminar discusses how these insights can inform reintegration policy, focusing on psychosocial support, gender equality and trust in democratic institutions. Ukraine is a democracy fighting a full-scale, prolonged defensive war on its own territory, making its experiences unique in modern times. At the same time, there are reasons to compare these experiences with other conflicts and draw lessons for the future.

content.title: From the frontline to the future – how is Ukrainian healthcare being rebuilt in the midst of war?
content.description: Russia's war has hit Ukraine's healthcare system hard. Yet rebuilding is taking place in the midst of active conflict. Sweden has a government mandate to support this process – but how does knowledge transfer work in practice, and what can Swedish organisations really deliver?
content.extendedDescription:
Russia's war has not only killed and injured hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians – it has systematically knocked out hospitals, ambulances, rehabilitation centres and the staff who run them. Yet rebuilding is taking place during the ongoing war: Ukrainian organisations are developing new care models adapted to wartime conditions, often without the resources that European healthcare takes for granted.
Since 2024, Sweden has had a government mandate to support the rebuilding of Ukraine's healthcare system – transferring Swedish knowledge and solutions to a country receiving them under fire. The question is no longer whether Sweden should contribute, but how: what works in practice, what do Swedish organisations fail to understand about Ukrainian conditions, and how can knowledge transfer remain effective when reality changes every day?

The discussion is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) – a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate.

content.title: How is AI-driven commerce changing consumption and retail?
content.description: At the beginning of the year, a new standard for AI-driven commerce called UCP was launched. This enables AI assistants to handle the entire customer journey, from discovery to direct purchase. Meanwhile, businesses without UCP support risk becoming invisible. How will this affect the way we shop and the entire industry?
content.extendedDescription:
As AI agents move from simple assistants to autonomous decision-makers, retail and society face a fundamental shift in power. One of the most pressing questions concerns personal autonomy: what happens to people's ability to make active choices when algorithms can curate and complete purchases for us? And what happens to businesses that are absent from the playing field when AI assistants scan the market?
There is also tension between efficiency and control: while agents can drive a resource-efficient, sustainable circular economy, they risk creating an opaque market in which people take a back seat. The question is how retailers and consumers should act to guide this development in the right direction.

content.title: From loneliness to community: what are the challenges and solutions?
content.description: Involuntary loneliness is a serious public health challenge, and the need for solutions is raised increasingly often. New meeting places are sought and new services developed. But we also need to pause and reflect: might many of the solutions already be right in front of us?
content.extendedDescription:
A range of initiatives already help people find community and new social settings. They bring people together around interests or everyday activities, taking the step from digital contact to meeting in real life.

Here, we highlight some initiatives already helping to reduce loneliness and strengthen social connections. You will encounter examples ranging from community-building apps developed by older people for older people to services for people who want to meet around shared interests.

We also explore how today's much-criticised digital platforms can actually provide an important bridge from social isolation into a social community.

Come and discover ways to build community, and try Speed-HEJ:ing, part of Hela Almedalen säger HEJ. In short sessions, you will meet randomly selected Almedalen visitors with different perspectives, experiences and opinions.

content.title: Has the region taken back control, and if so, how has this affected patients?
content.description: Following extensive changes to healthcare in Stockholm, several sources of evidence are now available to assess the results. Has the transition led to better access and equitable care, or to higher costs, reduced capacity and longer waiting lists for patients?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar takes as its starting point two recent reports analysing the consequences of healthcare policy in Region Stockholm during the 2022–2026 electoral term. Drawing on statistics, economic analyses and patient outcomes, it examines how changes in governance, patient choice systems and operating models have affected waiting lists, costs and access.

The discussion highlights the effects on the system when established healthcare capacity is closed down faster than new capacity is built, and how these choices affect patients with substantial care needs. It concludes by discussing lessons for future decisions on healthcare organisation and how resources can be used more effectively to reduce queues and improve outcomes for patients.

The seminar ends with a panel discussion featuring representatives of both the governing administration and the opposition in Region Stockholm.

content.title: The climate threat and climate policy — what do politicians want to know from researchers?
content.description: Climate change is one of the major challenges of our time. How is Sweden affected, what policies can address the climate crisis, and how effective are different policy instruments? In a time of uncertainty and rapid change, how can dialogue between science and politics be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
Politicians are often held to account in debates and panels, but what happens if we reverse the roles? In this seminar, Uppsala universitet gives politicians the opportunity to ask questions about climate change and policy instruments to a research panel comprising experts on both society and the environment. Possible questions include: How is Sweden affected? Which measures and policy instruments have the greatest impact? What obstacles prevent them from working effectively? How should conflicting goals be managed? The seminar aims to share scientific knowledge, strengthen dialogue between politicians and researchers, and create a platform where science and politics meet to discuss how the climate threat affects Sweden and what priorities are needed for a sustainable future.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: From ambition to practice — how do we develop public–private cooperation in civil defence?
content.description: Business is crucial to Sweden's security of supply and civil defence. Yet there is still no clear model for how the state and businesses should cooperate in practice. How do we move from ambitions for public–private cooperation to workable models?
content.extendedDescription:
There is broad ambition to strengthen public–private cooperation in civil defence. Yet a clear national model for organising this cooperation in practice is still lacking.

Several inquiries and strategies point to the need for new forms of cooperation, including security-of-supply agreements and other models to secure access to critical resources in crisis and war.

But how do we develop effective cooperation in practice?

This panel discussion takes that question as its starting point and explores how cooperation between the state, public authorities and business can develop in peacetime to strengthen Sweden's resilience. The focus is on practical models, the division of responsibilities and how solutions can be scaled nationally. The discussion is held in cooperation with Krisledningspodden, with Mats Bohman as moderator.

content.description: The EU has strengthened climate policy, but calls for lower ambitions are growing. Meanwhile, emissions are rising in several member states, including Sweden. content.extendedDescription:
The EU has substantially strengthened climate policy through the Green Deal and new legislation, but several member states are moving in the opposite direction. Calls to lower ambitions are growing while emissions increase, including in Sweden. This jeopardises climate targets and creates tensions between EU and national policy.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: Affordable housing in Sweden – how is it possible?
content.description: We need new solutions and affordable housing in Sweden. What alternatives exist, and can they be developed and scaled up?
content.extendedDescription:
We present different approaches already being used to provide more affordable housing for households that struggle to secure a home on their own. These are different methods that all work and help more households find a home where they can live well and stay.

Linda Lövgren from KTH presents the Kymmendö model; Cattis Carlén presents OBOS dela, a concept offering a more affordable model for buying a home; Johanna Lindroth explains how more people can gain access to suitable housing; and Helena Markgren, CEO of Skebo, presents how Skebo has developed affordable housing at scale, with 743 newly built affordable homes.

After the presentations, we discuss with our panel: how can these initiatives be scaled up, and what lessons can be learned? Where are the main barriers, and how do we overcome them? Where do policymakers need to intervene, and what is required for them to do so? Can the EU's affordable housing plan help us? What is the financing situation?

content.title: Meat and the climate – what does research say, and what are policymakers doing?
content.description: To meet climate targets, wealthy countries in particular need to reduce meat consumption. Meanwhile, the political debate about whether or not we should eat meat is heated. What complex challenges and conflicts surround the role of meat in the climate transition?
content.extendedDescription:
The food sector accounts for roughly a quarter of global greenhouse gas emissions. A large share comes from meat production and consumption. Research shows that meeting national and global climate targets requires reduced meat consumption, particularly in wealthy countries. Yet meat is a charged issue in public debate. Proposals to reduce consumption often provoke strong reactions and are frequently perceived as an intrusion into people's everyday lives or a threat to agriculture. This became apparent when Livsmedelsverket recently adjusted its dietary advice to a maximum of 350 grams per week.

Why does meat provoke such strong emotions? What role should politics play in what we eat? And what might the transition to a more sustainable food system look like in practice? This discussion brings together researchers, politicians and other stakeholders to discuss meat's place in the food systems of the future – and why the debate about whether or not to eat meat is so charged.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: It does not happen here – or does it? Abuse of power for sex in Sweden
content.description: How does sexual corruption manifest itself in Sweden? What blind spots exist in Swedish legislation, and what should we do about them?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is often perceived as one of the world's least corrupt and most gender-equal countries. Yet corruption in which sex is the currency occurs in Swedish public authorities, civil society organisations and companies.

Sexual corruption is the abuse of power for personal gain, with sex as the currency. Such corruption undermines trust in democratic institutions, even more than other forms of corruption. It is an old phenomenon but a new concept, now receiving attention on several fronts. Uppsala University Research Environment on Sexual Corruption (UU-RESC) studies this specific type of corruption. For two years, the UN has urged states to address corruption involving sex specifically. For the first time, sexual corruption is also highlighted in a Swedish context in the government inquiry into criminal-law measures against corruption and misconduct in public office (SOU 2025:87).

In this panel, researchers and anti-corruption experts discuss what corruption legislation is needed.

content.title: Sweden's nature — will it still be alive in 2050?
content.description: Nature is in a serious state; climate change and biodiversity loss are major societal problems. Sweden is subject to long-term environmental targets. Who should be responsible for nature in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Nature is in a serious state; climate change and biodiversity loss threaten a range of important societal functions. To reverse the trend for nature, Sweden is subject to several long-term climate and other environmental targets. As the EU Nature Restoration Regulation is implemented in Sweden, we therefore ask who should be responsible for nature in 2050.

These far-reaching targets raise questions about who is actually affected by long-term environmental policy and who can help achieve the goals. This panel brings together organisations that all work closely with Swedish nature to discuss future responsibility and implementation of the legislation. Who will have access to nature in 2050? Who has restoration expertise? How can different stakeholders come together to safeguard Swedish nature in the future?

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: Child poverty is increasing – how do we reverse the trend?
content.description: Many children in Sweden live in financial vulnerability. One in eight is affected, and many families experience serious financial anxiety. This can lead to financial risk-taking and debt. Meanwhile, the government's benefits reform risks increasing pressure on already vulnerable households. How can the trend be reversed?
content.extendedDescription:
How poverty is measured affects the picture, but the inequalities are clear. According to SCB, the number of people experiencing material and social poverty has doubled in five years, from 350,000 (2021) to more than 700,000 (2025). Single mothers are particularly vulnerable, with a sharp increase in the proportion affected. Meanwhile, most families with children live at what is classified as a high economic standard, illustrating growing disparities. Parents' financial stress affects children's security, health and future opportunities.
The seminar examines children's situation from a child rights perspective. Which political reforms can make the greatest difference, and who is responsible? How can civil society help reduce children's economic exclusion and create better conditions for growing up?

content.title: When war is already here – how can we strengthen Sweden's resilience in peacetime?
content.description: The war in Ukraine demonstrates the importance of an independent domestic defence industry, but also of civilian resilience, even in peacetime. Foreign powers launch cyberattacks daily against industry, banks and critical public infrastructure. How can preparedness in Sweden and Europe be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has demonstrated the importance of domestic and European defence industries in ensuring strategic freedom of action and rapid access to critical equipment. This is especially true when several international conflicts are taking place simultaneously and established alliance structures show signs of faltering. Sweden is certainly not at war, but as Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has pointed out, "nor is it at peace". Foreign powers launch cyberattacks daily against military and civilian industry to obtain strategic expertise and test systems' resilience. The same happens frequently to banking, electricity and telecommunications infrastructure, municipal water and wastewater facilities, healthcare and commercial businesses, for example in grocery retail.
This seminar discusses how Sweden's and Europe's military and civilian resilience can be increased, how the escalating threat to our sensitive IT infrastructure can be addressed, and, not least, the role of politics.

content.title: When security is procured at the lowest price – who takes responsibility for safety?
content.description: Security is a societal issue. When purchasing and procurement are driven too strongly by the lowest price, quality, responsibility and actual effectiveness risk being overlooked. This applies to both services and technology – from guarding to alarms, cameras, drones and integrated security solutions.
content.extendedDescription:
Security is not a standard product. Real safety depends on the right skills, relevant technology, effective management and a clear chain of responsibility. Several elements often need to work together: staff, alarms, cameras, analysis, supporting systems and the ability to act when something happens.
Yet much purchasing and procurement is characterised by price pressure, silos and requirements that do not always capture the actual security outcome. This risks disadvantaging responsible providers, holding back investment and ultimately providing poorer protection for people, organisations and essential infrastructure.

content.title: When young people are imprisoned today, who takes responsibility for their future tomorrow?
content.description: Crime has become a central issue for society, and new proposals seek tougher sentences, including for young people. At the same time, questions arise about human dignity and the future. What happens when a young person encounters the prison system, and who takes responsibility for life after the sentence?
content.extendedDescription:
As ever younger people are drawn into serious crime, demands on society's response are increasing. New proposals seek to make it possible to sentence children to prison for serious offences. This raises difficult questions about human dignity, responsibility and the future.
What happens to young people inside our prisons? And what happens when their sentence is over? Someone convicted as a child often has their whole life ahead of them. Who is responsible for the path forward?
The transition out of prison is often the most critical phase. Without support, young people risk returning to the same environments and patterns that led to the offence. Civil society plays an important role in supporting young people both during and after imprisonment, through conversation, community and practical support.
This is also about human worth, guilt and the possibility of reconciliation. What does it mean to speak of responsibility and justice while believing in people's capacity to change and make a new start? What can civil society, including the church, contribute after imprisonment? Who takes responsibility then?

content.title: Civil preparedness needs the security sector – when will the systems catch up?

content.title: Can disarmament and degrowth make us safer? Turning points and systemic change in a new era
content.description: In a time of increasing military build-up, climate crisis and growing inequality, new economic and political choices arise. Can monetary and tax reform, basic income and international disarmament initiatives create both safety and security, quality of life and climate justice?
content.extendedDescription:
As military spending rises and the climate crisis deepens, discussion is growing about alternative ways to organise the economy and security. Can a society become safer through disarmament rather than military build-up? What would basic income and degrowth mean in people's everyday lives?
In this conversation, we discuss possible political turning points:
• Can international guarantees of non-aggression replace military build-up?
• How can reduced resource consumption be combined with improved quality of life and social security?
• What would an unconditional basic income mean for work, freedom and the economy?
• Can economic reforms direct investment away from exploitation and increased energy use and towards ecological transition and reduced inequality?
What do these ideas mean in practice, and what objections are there?
To prepare, we recommend the podcast "Samtal om vändpunkter" on our website, featuring in-depth discussions of these turning points. (1 of 5 seminars. Search for Partiet Vändpunkt to see all the seminars.)

content.title: Investigating war crimes in Ukraine – how do we document them and hold Russia accountable?
content.description: Since 2022, Ukrainian and international organisations have documented thousands of war crimes. Arrest warrants have been issued. Yet most perpetrators remain at large. What stands in the way from documentation to conviction – and what can Sweden do?
content.extendedDescription:
Thousands of war crimes have been documented in Ukraine since 2022 – hospital bombings, torture, executions and deportations. The ICC has so far issued arrest warrants for six Russian individuals – including Putin, Shoigu and Gerasimov – for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine. Yet the road from documentation to conviction is long and uncertain. What prevents effective accountability?
This discussion focuses on documentation in practice: how is evidence collected during active conflict, what is required for it to stand up in international courts, and what role do Ukrainian and Swedish civil society play in advancing accountability?

The discussion is organised as part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) – a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: Osteoporosis – a neglected investment
content.description: On unequal care, growing waiting lists and why better care matters from a societal perspective. Despite affecting so many people, the disease remains both underdiagnosed and undertreated. How can we improve care and reduce unnecessary suffering?
content.extendedDescription:
Osteoporosis is one of our major common diseases and causes more than 100 000 fractures every year in Sweden. It primarily affects older people, more often women, and leads to considerable pain, poorer quality of life, disability and increased mortality. For society, this places a substantial burden on healthcare and social care.
Waiting times for assessment vary greatly between regions. Many patients are not identified after their first fracture, which often leads to repeated, frequently preventable fractures and resulting increases in costs and care needs.
Clear national guidelines and effective treatment strategies are available today and have been shown to reduce the risk of further fractures. Despite this, only a small proportion of patients receive adequate secondary prevention within a year of a fracture.
Join a discussion about how osteoporosis care can become more equitable, preventive and sustainable in the long term, and why this should be seen as an investment rather than a cost.

content.title: What is required of Ukrainian trade unions on the path towards the EU?
content.description: Ukraine's path towards the EU requires far-reaching reforms – including within trade unions. The war has eroded workers' rights, fragmented the labour market and put EU harmonisation on hold. What must Ukrainian trade unions do to meet EU requirements – and what do they need to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine's EU candidacy requires the harmonisation of labour law, collective bargaining rights and social dialogue structures. But the war has changed the conditions: martial law has temporarily suspended labour protections, millions of workers have fled or lost their jobs, and parts of industry have been destroyed. Ukrainian trade unions are caught in this contradiction – they must be strengthened and reformed to align with the EU while operating in a country under active invasion. How can they navigate the EU's social rules when reality changes every day?
This discussion explores what moving towards the EU specifically requires of Ukrainian trade unions, what structural barriers exist, and what Sweden and European actors can contribute to support the process.

The discussion is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) – a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate.

content.title: The new charging economy: from challenge to business value
content.description: Electrification is happening here and now, but access to charging is deeply unequal. Technology and grants are in place. Yet too many property owners are waiting. To meet the 2030 targets, more must act now, not later.
content.extendedDescription:
What will it take for property owners, energy companies and the automotive industry to pull in the same direction? Around 70% of all vehicle emissions come from private cars. Yet most people living in apartment buildings lack access to reasonable charging facilities. This is not a technology problem or a grant problem. It is a decision-making problem.

At this breakfast seminar, we demonstrate that profitable charging is already possible, without waiting for power regulations, V2G or the next generation of technology. Everything needed is already in place.

We begin with an interactive session in which the audience shares its own views. We then take a broad look at the facts, practical experience and the questions that actually determine whether the transition gathers pace. This is followed by a panel discussion on smart charging, energy optimisation, V2G and making charging accessible to more people.

The aim is for you to leave the breakfast table with concrete next steps, not more unanswered questions.

Breakfast sandwiches and coffee from 07:45. Welcome.

content.title: 200,000 more hours of leadership – can broader collaboration create the care of the future?
content.description: Care managers face growing documentation requirements, tighter regulations and increasing needs. Meanwhile, time for hands-on leadership is more important than ever as the pace of change keeps accelerating. How can this equation work?
content.extendedDescription:
Ambea has implemented AI support at scale and now frees up almost 200,000 management hours annually. Investigation times have halved, recruitment processes shortened and administration simplified. Technology enhances people rather than replacing them.
As one of the Nordic region's largest care providers, Ambea has shown that AI can be implemented at scale. What is needed for others to make the same journey?
Can the private sector serve as a testbed and development driver for the entire care sector? How do we create more partnerships that accelerate implementation in real operations?

In this panel, municipal, private-provider and academic representatives discuss how partnerships can accelerate implementation. How do we create more partnerships where municipalities, academia and the private sector share risk, learning and results?

content.title: Can disarmament and degrowth make us safer? Turning points and systemic change in a new era
content.description: In a time of increasing military build-up, climate crisis and growing inequality, new economic and political choices arise. Can monetary and tax reform, basic income and international disarmament initiatives create both safety and security, quality of life and climate justice?
content.extendedDescription:
As military spending rises and the climate crisis deepens, discussion is growing about alternative ways to organise the economy and security. Can a society become safer through disarmament rather than military build-up? What would basic income and degrowth mean in people's everyday lives?
In this conversation, we discuss possible political turning points:
• Can international guarantees of non-aggression replace military build-up?
• How can reduced resource consumption be combined with improved quality of life and social security?
• What would an unconditional basic income mean for work, freedom and the economy?
• Can economic reforms direct investment away from exploitation and increased energy use and towards ecological transition and reduced inequality?
What do these ideas mean in practice, and what objections are there?
To prepare, we recommend the podcast "Samtal om vändpunkter" on our website, featuring in-depth discussions of these turning points. (1 of 5 seminars. Search for Partiet Vändpunkt to see all the seminars.)

content.title: A vibrant city centre is a matter of growth, not just enjoyment
content.description: A vibrant city centre is a matter of growth, not just enjoyment. Strong city centres attract people, skills and investment, creating jobs and a tax base. What is needed to make city centres part of the infrastructure for growth, in line with the government's strategy for vibrant and safe cities?
content.extendedDescription:
The city centre is not a nostalgic postcard. It is the region's engine of growth and hub for commerce, workplaces, investment and attractiveness. Property values, shop openings and hotel rooms indicate whether capital and skills want to stay or move away.

Behaviours and the economy are changing rapidly. E-commerce, hybrid working and demographic changes affect movement, consumption and safety needs. When more people want to live, work, invest and spend time in city centres, synergies emerge that strengthen industries and contribute to long-term development.

The seminar focuses on how to achieve this in practice. What political decisions, policy instruments and local initiatives are needed for lasting effects? The discussion covers mixed uses, mobility, simpler regulations and cooperation between municipalities, property owners, businesses and civil society.

content.title: How can the railway sector help reduce unemployment in Sweden?
content.description: Sweden faces both growing unemployment and an urgent need for technical skills. Meanwhile, the railway sector is undergoing a historic expansion, with modernisation, maintenance and sustainable transport of the future requiring more skilled professionals than ever.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar discusses how the railway sector can become a strategic force in reducing unemployment by offering educational pathways, secure careers and routes into a growing profession of the future. How can industry, authorities, education providers and society work together to match people with opportunities and secure the skills that keep Sweden moving?

Panel 1 – Who builds Sweden? Does the skills shortage threaten implementation of the national plan? What is being done today, and what investment is needed to succeed?

Panel 2 – Railways as an industry of the future: future skills supply, innovation, digitalisation and collaboration.

Panel 3 – Railway skills supply from a total defence perspective: passenger transport, freight and total defence needs – are these interests compatible? How are measures prioritised, who funds them and how will skills be secured?

content.title: The Tidö Pact – the agreement's consequences for Swedish politics and democracy
content.description: The Tidö Agreement meant that Moderaterna, Kristdemokraterna and Liberalerna abandoned their previous refusal to cooperate with Sverigedemokraterna. Why did they change their minds? And what does the agreement mean for democracy in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden was long an exception in Europe. A right-wing parliamentary majority refused to cooperate with a populist radical-right party, allowing a red–green minority government to govern instead. Sweden is no longer an exception. Through the Tidö Agreement, Sverigedemokraterna has been normalised.
The book “Tidöpakten. Så förändras Sverige” (Atlas, 2026) examines different explanations for what happened. Did pressure from members and voters of Moderaterna, Kristdemokraterna and Liberalerna become too strong for their leaders to resist? Or has Sverigedemokraterna changed? Is the party no longer coloured by its ideological roots, removing its pariah status?
Does the Tidö Agreement erode legal certainty and individual rights and freedoms in ways that contradict liberal democracy? What do research and established experience say about strategies established parties can use to counter the growing political strength of populist radical-right parties?

content.title: The cancer strategy has been adopted – but how do we measure its success?
content.description: The new national cancer strategy sets goals for greater survival, better quality of life and more equitable care. But how do we know whether it actually improves patient outcomes? Which indicators are needed to track developments in cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
The national cancer strategy sets goals to improve prevention, earlier detection, more effective treatment and quality of life for people living with or after cancer.
To make a real difference, monitoring must reflect what matters most to patients and society. Cancer care is often measured using process indicators, such as adherence to care guidelines, rather than outcomes such as survival, quality of life and equitable access to innovation.
As cancer care moves towards more personalised diagnosis and treatment, a central question arises: what do we actually need to measure to ensure the strategy delivers real patient benefit?
The seminar brings stakeholders from across cancer care together to discuss translating the strategy's goals into concrete, meaningful indicators.

content.title: How can historic environments develop sustainably in an era of climate change and transition?
content.description: Historic environments are affected by climate change, social transformation and new demands on their use. How can they be developed and managed sustainably without losing their value? This requires new approaches and knowledge that can address both preservation and change.
content.extendedDescription:

The event is aimed at decision-makers, public authorities and organisations working in the built environment, cultural heritage and urban development.

content.title: Attractiveness, identity and energy efficiency in properties with cultural heritage value
content.description: Renovating existing buildings is crucial to reducing society's climate and energy impact. Yet many properties have cultural and historical values requiring sensitive development. How can energy efficiency improvements strengthen rather than weaken buildings' identity and quality?
content.extendedDescription:
How can energy efficiency improvements be made in buildings of cultural and historical value without losing their identity and heritage? This question is central to the climate transition and requires cooperation between property owners, architects, energy experts and heritage specialists.

The seminar explores how cooperation between energy expertise, architecture and conservation expertise can create solutions that both reduce climate impact and improve buildings' appeal and usefulness.

Examples and experience inform a discussion of the analyses, decision-making evidence and working methods that can help property owners make sustainable decisions. The discussion also covers the expertise and documentation that can be requested in dialogue between property owners, consultants and permitting authorities.

The event is aimed at property owners, developers, public organisations and others managing and developing buildings of cultural and historical value.

content.title: AI and health data – are we finally moving from vision to reality in cancer care?
content.description: AI and advanced data analysis can support earlier detection, more accurate treatment decisions and better follow-up in cancer care. But fragmented IT systems, unclear regulations and limited data sharing currently impede progress. How can we create more data-driven cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
Cancer is one of today's greatest public health challenges, with cases expected to rise as the population ages. Meanwhile, new diagnostic methods, treatments and data-driven tools are developing rapidly. For patients to benefit, healthcare must use health data more effectively, securely and systematically than today.
Sweden has strong foundations in national registries, digital maturity and research. Yet major barriers remain to sharing, analysing and using health data in clinical practice, quality monitoring and research. Poor interoperability, unclear regulations and fragmented IT systems prevent the full potential of AI and advanced data analysis from being realised.
The seminar discusses how AI and better use of health data can support earlier detection, more personalised diagnosis and better treatment decisions, and how Sweden can benefit from initiatives such as the European Health Data Space.

content.title: Do we need a coordinated policy for nature?
content.description: Biodiversity loss threatens Sweden's welfare. Does Sweden need a legal nature policy framework that, like the climate policy framework, supports a societal transition for biodiversity? What do the parliamentary parties think?
content.extendedDescription:
Addressing the nature crisis and meeting Sweden's commitments to protect biodiversity requires a societal transition to which everyone contributes, from citizens to businesses and policymakers.

For almost a decade, a climate policy framework has included a Climate Act, climate targets and a Climate Policy Council. It has helped make climate a central political issue. Is a similar framework needed to counter biodiversity loss and give nature a more central place on the political agenda?

The seminar presents a proposed legal nature policy framework and what it could mean. The presentation forms the basis for a discussion between representatives of several parliamentary parties.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Climate transition in rural Sweden – is it possible?
content.description: Sweden's rural areas are portrayed as bottlenecks in the climate debate. But what do people living there actually think? How can policy facilitate the transition throughout the country? What do researchers, political parties and other stakeholders say?
content.extendedDescription:
Debates about the climate transition often claim that policy penalises rural residents in particular. Claims that transition problems are especially severe in rural areas frequently justify dismantling climate policy, especially concerning climate and transport. But what do rural residents and the organisations representing them actually think? Can the transport system change in ways that also benefit rural areas? What public investment and policy instruments are needed? What do researchers, political parties and other stakeholders say?

The seminar begins with presentations by researchers and representatives of different parts of civil society, focusing on co-created climate policy for rural transitions. In the next part, political party representatives discuss the proposals presented.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitets klimatdagar.

content.title: Young people and financial security: from first job to retirement
content.description: Young people today often face a tough financial start: difficulties entering the housing market, an uncertain labour market and growing debt. Meanwhile, pensions take shape early because lifetime earnings determine them. How can young people build long-term security and reduce risks, and what reforms could strengthen their financial health?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden's pension system rests on a contract between generations. The idea is simple: you work, pay into the system and can then rely on a reasonable pension when you grow older. But much has changed, and responsibility for pensions rests more heavily on individuals than before. Today's young people study longer, enter the labour market later and often start their working lives in insecure jobs. Meanwhile, each generation lives longer, increasing the need to work longer.

content.title: Hospital at home – can advanced cancer care move into patients' homes?
content.description: More people are living for a long time with cancer, and new treatments make care at home or close to home possible. This requires collaboration, new ways of working and clear rules on responsibility, funding and patient safety. How can hospital-at-home services develop within cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
More patients are living for a long time with or after a cancer diagnosis. Meanwhile, new treatments, digital follow-up and medical technologies make advanced care possible at home or close to patients' homes. For many patients, this can improve quality of life and reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.
International experience shows that treatment at home can be delivered safely when care is organised properly and multiple stakeholders collaborate. However, this development raises questions about responsibility, reimbursement systems, skills supply and collaboration between regions and municipal home healthcare.

The seminar starts from patients' vision of being treated at home when possible and in hospital when necessary. Examples from ongoing initiatives inform a discussion of the organisational and regulatory changes needed to bring future cancer care closer to patients.

content.title: Preparedness and geopolitics make cancer care and cancer research a security issue
content.description: In a new security-policy environment, cancer care, medicines, medical technology and health data become part of society's critical infrastructure. How do we ensure robust care, research and clinical trials even in crisis and war – and how does life science strengthen Sweden's resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
As competitiveness becomes increasingly linked to security policy, cancer care, research and innovation need to be seen as part of society's critical infrastructure. Vulnerable supply chains, dependence on advanced medical technology and increasing cyber threats mean that diagnostics, medicines, radiotherapy and health data must be integrated into Sweden's civil preparedness.

At the same time, questions arise about how research and clinical trials can continue even when healthcare resources are under pressure. How do we ensure patients retain access to new treatments and Sweden maintains its international position in life science?
The seminar discusses how cancer care can be integrated into national preparedness and total defence planning.

Scenario-based panel discussions examine cancer care as critical societal infrastructure, medicines supply and medical technology as strategic resources, and how research, data resources and international partnerships can strengthen the system's resilience.

content.title: Unexpected collaborations – the key to future cancer care and innovation?
content.description: What can we do together that no actor can achieve alone? Today's and tomorrow's cancer challenges require collaboration between research, healthcare, business, civil society and patients. Unexpected partnerships can deliver faster innovation, more effective prevention and better support for everyone with cancer.
content.extendedDescription:
An inspiring, interactive session focusing on unexpected collaborations between organisations and sectors. Through concrete examples, we explore how new partnerships can contribute to prevention, innovation and better health. We look at initiatives combining culture and vaccination, clinical trials and learning, physical activity and patient support, social relationships and mental health, and grocery retail, local produce and healthy food choices.

The session includes networking and opportunities to establish new contacts and collaborations. Hesselby Jernvägscafé serves locally produced food and drinks during the event.

Programme:
• Combining benefit and pleasure – HPV vaccination at the cinema
• Learning for life – the clinical trials of the future
• Discovering strength – boxing and prostate cancer
• Friendship care – new approaches to social relationships and health
• Good advice need not be expensive – news from the fruit counter and pasta shelf
• Are we ready for kick-off? – a closing discussion about Sweden's next steps in the EU Cancer Mission

content.title: When children's influence declines and demands for tougher measures grow – how is young people's confidence in the future affected?
content.description: Young people describe how inequality and limited influence create mistrust. When decisions do not reflect their reality, trust in politics weakens. How can young people's confidence in the future be strengthened when children's rights receive less attention?
content.extendedDescription:
Young people describe a growing gap between their reality and political decisions. Through workshops, surveys and analysis, a youth reference group has identified areas where trust, respect and participation are lacking. The findings show a need for better feedback, clearer accountability, faster processes on issues affecting young people, and a more respectful climate of discussion.

The seminar is led by the young people themselves, who formulate the questions and set the framework based on their analyses. Politicians participate to listen, respond and reflect on how children's rights can have greater practical impact. The discussion covers participation, unequal living conditions, the role of schools, online safety and how political language affects young people's confidence in the future. The aim is to move from symbolic initiatives to real accountability that strengthens young people's trust in democracy.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: How can police support for victims of crime be improved?
content.description: Despite the government's rhetoric about a paradigm shift placing victims of crime at the centre, support for victims has major shortcomings. British police have made their support for victims more effective. What can Swedish police learn from British experience?
content.extendedDescription:
A paradigm shift for Sweden: that is one way to summarise the government's justice policy. In a short time, numerous inquiries and a series of new laws and legislative proposals have been presented. Victims of crime are rarely mentioned, and when they are, it is easy to get the impression that this is primarily to justify tougher sentences. But what is the situation facing victims, and what help, support and protection do they need? At the seminar, British police describe how new systems, data-driven processes, new working methods and a change in culture have rapidly made information and support for victims more effective. The result is sharply reduced waiting times and increased trust in the police. What can Swedish police learn from British experience, and how can support for victims be improved?

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF).

content.title: Sweden should send peace doves — not bombs
content.description: As major powers build up their armed forces and conflicts deepen, the language of peace becomes more important than ever. Diplomacy is not weakness. It is the courage to choose dialogue over confrontation and cooperation over conflict.
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, rearmament and armed conflict, we need more spaces where the voice of peace can be heard. In this workshop, participants are invited to fold peace doves and write personal messages about peace, dialogue and international cooperation.

The collected messages will then be compiled and presented to Sweden's Minister for Defence as a symbolic reminder of the importance of safeguarding diplomacy, human security and peaceful solutions to global conflicts.
As the world faces difficult choices, we need to ask ourselves: How do we create conditions for dialogue as divisions grow? How do we ensure that conversation and cooperation have more space than confrontation and mistrust?

Diplomacy is not passivity. It is active work to prevent conflicts and build lasting peace. Through this workshop, we want to give participants the opportunity to contribute their own perspectives and jointly highlight the importance of the language of peace in troubled times.

content.title: Insider threat prevention and background checks against organised crime
content.description: Insider threats and improper influence are societal problems with serious consequences and links to organised crime. They are spreading and infiltrating companies. At a time when confidence matters more than ever, we want a society built on trust. How can we strengthen our organisations?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar focuses on one of organisations' most underestimated risks: threats arising from within, and how work to create safer workplaces becomes a crucial part of the solution.

The human factor is both one of an organisation's greatest vulnerabilities and its greatest assets. Managing this complexity requires more than checks, policies and technical safeguards: it takes conscious leadership, an open culture and the right knowledge.

Internal culture – security culture – is increasingly important for strengthening protection against criminal infiltration. Employers face difficult trade-offs: where is the boundary between security, privacy and social responsibility?

In this session, experts discuss identity and background checks, risk assessment and leadership to develop safe workplaces.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and SOFF.

content.title: Why has Sweden abandoned Palme's peace policy?
content.description: Sweden was long a voice for peace and diplomacy. What does that role look like today?
content.extendedDescription:
During Olof Palme's time, Sweden played a prominent role in international peace policy and efforts towards dialogue, disarmament and conflict resolution. Today's world looks different, with new security policy challenges and heightened international tensions. What role can Sweden play in future peace efforts?

A podcast conversation discussing these issues will be recorded on site during this session. It focuses on Sweden's opportunities to contribute to peace, diplomacy and conflict resolution in a changing world, and the lessons that can be learned from earlier generations' peace work.

content.title: Sweden should send peace doves, not bombs
content.description: As major powers build up their armed forces and conflicts deepen, the language of peace becomes more important than ever. Diplomacy is not weakness. It is the courage to choose dialogue over confrontation and cooperation over conflict.
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, rearmament and armed conflict, we need more spaces where the voice of peace can be heard. In this workshop, participants are invited to fold peace doves and write personal messages about peace, dialogue and international cooperation. The collected messages will then be compiled and presented to Sweden's Minister for Defence as a symbolic reminder of the importance of safeguarding diplomacy, human security and peaceful solutions to global conflicts.

As the world faces difficult choices, we need to ask ourselves: How do we create conditions for dialogue as divisions grow? How do we ensure that conversation and cooperation have more space than confrontation and mistrust?

Diplomacy is not passivity. It is active work to prevent conflicts and build lasting peace. In this workshop, we fold peace doves and write messages about the future we want to see.

content.title: Security in transition: how do we tackle crime against people, businesses and organisations?
content.description: Crime against businesses and organisations is a growing problem. Four in ten businesses report having experienced crime in the past year, according to Brå. How can security work evolve as threats change? And how can cooperation between the police, public authorities and business be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
Security and insecurity are among our greatest societal challenges. In this session, decision-makers and the organisers of SäkerhetsArenan discuss what is needed in the work ahead to keep our society safe.

Traditional security measures involving alarms, locks and cameras now need to be complemented by new approaches. Cybersecurity, identity checks, risk assessments and structured security work are becoming increasingly important in protecting operations and societal functions.

How can security work evolve to address new threats? How can cooperation between the police, public authorities and business be strengthened? And how can different security measures be combined to provide more effective protection against crime?

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF).

content.title: Cybersecurity and resilience – how do we protect society in a digital age?
content.description: Cybersecurity threats against Sweden and critical societal operations are increasing. How do we ensure we can withstand attacks and ransomware from different threat actors and foreign powers? How can society strengthen its resilience when technology creates both opportunities and new vulnerabilities?
content.extendedDescription:
Digitalisation has created major opportunities for society and business, but also new vulnerabilities. Cyberattacks, ransomware and other digital attacks now target companies, public authorities and essential services alike.

In this session, we speak with leading experts in information security, IT and cybersecurity to explore both technological and human needs.

content.title: Sweden should send peace doves, not bombs
content.description: As great powers rearm and conflicts deepen, the language of peace becomes more important than ever. Diplomacy is not weakness. It is the courage to choose dialogue over confrontation and cooperation over conflict.
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, rearmament and armed conflict, more spaces are needed for the voice of peace. In this workshop, participants are invited to fold peace doves and formulate personal messages about peace, dialogue and international cooperation.

The collected messages will then be compiled and delivered to Sweden's Minister for Defence as a symbolic reminder of the importance of diplomacy, human security and peaceful solutions to global conflicts.

As the world faces difficult choices, we must ask: how do we create conditions for dialogue when divisions grow?

Diplomacy is not passivity. It is active work to prevent conflict and build lasting peace. Through this workshop, we want to enable participants to contribute their own perspectives and jointly highlight the importance of the language of peace in troubled times.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Creating producer responsibility for textiles – what producers need
content.description: The EU's revised Waste Directive entered into force in autumn 2025 and must be fully implemented in Sweden by 2028. This means that businesses will have to cover the costs of collecting and sorting textiles and textile waste.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar on the latest developments in producer responsibility for textiles!
Work on designing Swedish producer responsibility for textiles and footwear is now at a decisive stage, as the Waste Directive must be implemented within two years. The issue is how the textile and fashion industry can transition to more sustainable and circular business models while maintaining its competitiveness. The design of Swedish producer responsibility for textiles will have consequences for both Swedish businesses and consumers.

Svensk Handel and TEKO, Sveriges Textil- och modeföretag therefore invite you to a seminar on the current state of the process. We identify the key issues ahead and highlight the potential consequences of the decisions to be made. During the seminar, a panel representing different parts of the textile value chain will discuss the issue from their perspectives.
