content.title: Can we live healthy lives in an unhealthy society?
content.description: Stress, mental ill health and lifestyle-related diseases are increasing as inequality grows. How do societal structures affect people's health? How can economic democracy contribute to better public health?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more Swedes experience stress, mental ill health and reduced quality of life. Research also shows that economic divides, insecure living conditions and limited influence over one's daily life can affect health and wellbeing. How are societal structures, the economy and public health connected? And what reforms are needed to create a healthier, more sustainable society?
During this session, a podcast discussing these questions will be recorded on site. The conversation addresses the links between public health, economic democracy and social security, and how greater citizen influence over societal development can improve living conditions. It will also explore how healthcare policy can be reformed to become more accessible, preventive, equitable and patient-centred, with the aim of providing care that better meets people's needs nationwide.
Drawing on the social ideas of the Swedish ‘people's home’, the discussion also considers how a modern society can strengthen both physical and mental health.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Healthcare's biggest headache, and the remedy
content.description: Healthcare must become more accessible, closer, better and ideally cheaper as needs keep growing. What belongs on the election agenda: digital working conditions, extra funding to support new ways of working, or better obesity care? How should Swedish healthcare be governed, organised and funded?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish healthcare is in transition. Care should move closer to patients, more treatment should take place at home and highly specialised care should concentrate in fewer units. New patient record systems change working conditions, often provoking strong professional reactions. Meanwhile, fundamental questions grow: what role should private actors play in future care? Where should the boundary between public and private funding lie?
Is nostalgia obstructing the shift to care closer to patients? Despite broad agreement on person-centred care and substantial investment, progress is barely noticeable. What innovations do primary and inpatient care need now to connect the patient's journey, and how can they happen? What political governance is needed? Which dreams must be abandoned to move forward?
A new era for obesity care: have medicines made old advice irrelevant? How must healthcare change its working methods to help patients?

content.title: We personal assistance users face several existential threats: will we be able to continue living freely?
content.description: For those of us with significant disabilities, the right to personal assistance, and therefore our freedom, is constantly threatened. Personal assistance is the only form of support that meets the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. We are survivors, but will we be able to keep living like everyone else?
content.extendedDescription:
The 1994 personal assistance reform enabled many of us to avoid institutional living. With assistance, we could finally live like other citizens, take our place in society and participate on our own terms. But over the years, savings requirements and case law have severely restricted our freedom. Obtaining personal assistance has become increasingly difficult, and those receiving this vital support constantly worry that their assistance hours will be withdrawn.

The ability to choose a family member as an assistant and to hold dual roles as assistant, legal representative and supervisor is threatened. Who is better placed to support a person with an intellectual disability in making decisions than someone who knows them well, often a family member?

The personal assistance allowance is critically low. It must now be increased substantially, to exactly SEK 400, and then linked to a wage index. The Chair of Riksföreningen JAG gives the opening address in the JAG tent.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Urgently restoring personal assistance allowance: exactly SEK 400
content.description: By failing to increase personal assistance allowance in line with wage rises and other costs, successive Swedish governments are deliberately starving this vital reform of funding. How much longer can responsible providers survive?
content.extendedDescription:
SEK 347.70. That is the hourly personal assistance allowance: the amount Försäkringskassan pays, which must cover not only wages and employer contributions but also training, overheads, insurance and administration.

Over the past decade, successive Swedish governments have allowed the allowance to fall behind wage increases and inflation. For 2025–2026, collectively agreed wage rises amount to 6.4 per cent. The Tidö parties increased the allowance by 4.5 per cent over those two years. Its erosion is a fact. It cannot be news to any Member of Parliament responsible for social and financial issues that the funding no longer covers high-quality, safe personal assistance.

The funding is no longer sufficient to provide reasonable conditions for personal assistants, a good induction for new employees, or ongoing professional development and supervision. These are vital ingredients in high-quality assistance.

Are politicians killing off the reform without changing the law?

content.title: Healthcare crisis or transformation? Parkinson's patient numbers expected to double by 2040 – how do we ensure equitable care?
content.description: Parkinson's is the fastest-growing neurological disease. 22 000 people live with the diagnosis, and many more are affected. Every hour counts. Timely, appropriate care determines functioning and quality of life. Technology and guidelines exist; political will and organisational structures are now needed. Who takes responsibility and leads the way?
content.extendedDescription:
Parkinson's is a disease in which every hour without appropriate care can permanently impair functioning and quality of life. Despite medical advances, place of residence often determines the care received. Socialstyrelsen's 2025 evaluation shows we are far from achieving equitable care: only 60% see their neurologist once a year, despite guidelines recommending two annual visits, and regional differences are substantial. Resource shortages affect follow-up, assessment, care interventions and quality of life.

We need to move from passive waiting to active follow-up and action based on need. Achieving Socialstyrelsen's goals requires a structured care pathway that identifies patients' medical needs in time. The seminar discusses innovative methods and proactive triage that can improve Parkinson's care, use healthcare resources more efficiently, shorten waiting lists and provide care according to patients' needs rather than fixed schedules. The right care at the right time saves society's resources.

Breakfast is served.

content.title: The global humanitarian system in crisis and reform: how do we do more with less, and do it better?
content.description: The world faces record humanitarian needs while funding falls and millions go without support. This has put the global humanitarian system under intense pressure, leading to difficult priorities and extensive ongoing reforms. How should Swedish aid develop in this new context?
content.extendedDescription:
Humanitarian needs are at a record high. More than 120 armed conflicts are ongoing, 123 million people are displaced and 305 million need urgent support. Meanwhile, major donors are reducing their support and the UN faces a deep funding crisis. At this critical moment, we are forced to rethink and find new approaches.

Against this backdrop, a new design for the humanitarian system has taken shape – The Humanitarian Reset – with clearer recognition of local actors' role, a stronger focus on anticipatory action and higher demands for cost efficiency. Meanwhile, major shifts are taking place in development aid globally and within the EU. How Sweden and the Swedish organisations and expertise involved in aid respond to this paradigm shift, addressing its challenges and opportunities, will determine the future of aid. How do we do more with less without compromising humanitarian principles?

Sweden is in an election year, and several political parties promise further reform and a new aid agenda. How should Swedish aid develop in this new context, and how does it compare with other donors and the EU?

content.title: What makes neighbourhood collaboration work, and what does it mean in practice?
content.description: How can areas develop through neighbourhood collaboration?
content.extendedDescription:
Bergsjön in Gothenburg is one of Sweden's particularly vulnerable areas. Yet reported crime has fallen by 27 per cent and the share of residents feeling safe has risen from 60 to 88 per cent. In the report Bergsjön i rörelse, Bergsjön 2031 analyses the district's development between 2015 and 2025.

Since 2011, Bergsjön 2031 has brought residents, property owners, the municipality, police and civil society together around shared development work. The seminar starts from the results and focuses on fifteen years of neighbourhood collaboration and long-term district development.

What makes long-term collaboration work? What has succeeded, what has been difficult, and what experiences might be relevant elsewhere?

We discuss these questions with representatives who have authority and expertise in the issues.

content.title: From bicycle storage to civil defence shelter in 100 days
content.description: Sweden's crisis preparedness is being tested in an increasingly uncertain world. Thousands of civil defence shelters exist, but many are effectively unusable today. Given the maintenance backlog, regulatory barriers and inadequate supply chains, how can shelters be made operational quickly?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden currently has around 64,000 civil defence shelters, but many have become bicycle storage rooms, storerooms and association premises.
As the international situation changes rapidly, shelters have returned to the spotlight, but awareness and confidence are low: more than half of Swedes do not know where their nearest shelter is, and 78 per cent have little confidence that shelters work.
Yet shelters are an active part of our civil defence and a tangible resource that can make a difference in a crisis. To fulfil their purpose, municipalities, authorities, property owners and businesses must collaborate. This means surveying, refurbishing and restoring shelters, securing material supplies, providing training on regulations and creating long-term maintenance plans.
How can we move from awareness to action? What is needed to open Sweden's shelters? These questions are addressed in today's seminar, where we discuss concrete steps to strengthen Sweden's preparedness.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.description: Is wasting taxpayers' money just about municipalities buying pink unicorns or a swimming pool running over budget – or is it a systemic failure? Where do the wasted billions go? content.title: Personal assistance – a form of life insurance for every citizen
content.description: Anyone can become one of us at any time. No one knows what awaits around the next corner. A wrong step into the street, a serious illness? But Sweden has a unique safety net. No other country offers this kind of assurance that you can continue to live like others despite major disabilities.
content.extendedDescription:
Personal assistance provides security for both families and individuals that you did not know you might need. A single moment can change everything. Yesterday it was me; tomorrow it could be you or someone you love. A wrong step into the street, a misjudged turn on a ski slope, a riding accident, ALS or a stroke in middle age can lead to both physical and intellectual disabilities, where the right to personal assistance enables you to remain in your home and with your family and live a good life.

A vital reform, unique in its kind, for which Sweden is known worldwide. In the JAG tent, you can meet JAG members and learn more about human rights and why personal assistance is a vital service. Welcome!
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Do Jews need to flee Sweden?
content.description: What are the parliamentary parties doing to counter rampant antisemitism in Sweden? After Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, both Sweden and the rest of the Western world were taken by surprise by the strong antisemitic currents that were suddenly exposed.
content.extendedDescription:
Good values and acceptance of objective truths are important foundations for a safe and prosperous society. It is the free market in the Western world that has created these conditions and built strong, prosperous societies with Western values and culture.

When people reach for simple explanations of societal problems, socialism and collectivism are close at hand, and these are precisely the ideologies now joining forces with antisemitic movements originating primarily in the Middle East. content.title: Innovation developed in Sweden — built for the world
content.description: Europe faces a choice: compete with yesterday's technology or lead the development of the next generation of energy-efficient transport? How do we ensure that innovation developed in Sweden is not only exported globally, but also used and scaled at home?
content.extendedDescription:
How does Europe build industry amid intensifying global competition?

In this seminar, we discuss how technology developed and built in Sweden can strengthen Europe's competitiveness, reduce energy use and create new sustainable transport systems.

The discussion starts with electric hydrofoil vessels and developments in energy-efficient maritime transport, but is fundamentally about something bigger: how advanced engineering, software and sustainable production can become Sweden's next export success while creating future jobs and industrial expertise in Sweden and Europe.

content.title: How do we create good, cost-effective living environments for an ageing population?
content.description: Sweden's population is ageing, increasing the need for secure, socially sustainable and affordable housing. Meanwhile, municipalities face high costs, growing home-care needs and loneliness among older people. Can converting apartment buildings into co-housing communities create companionship, security and lower costs?
content.extendedDescription:
Good living environments for older people are one of today's major societal issues. Traditional solutions, such as newly built sheltered housing, are often expensive, take a long time to deliver and reach a limited group. Research also shows that loneliness and a lack of social connection affect older people's health and security as much as access to formal care.

The seminar presents an alternative strategy: converting more existing apartment buildings into co-housing communities for older people. These communities can provide everyday companionship, increase security and strengthen the feeling of being needed. Their social structure can also reduce municipal home-care needs through mutual everyday support.

Using the existing housing stock can make the transition faster than building new homes. Conversion often costs less and makes it possible to keep rents affordable for more people. Co-housing can therefore become an option for a broader group of older people.

content.title: The wind industry – a blight on rural areas
content.description: Wind power is often presented as a green solution, but for many people in rural areas it means something very different. Large-scale wind power changes landscapes, affects natural assets and creates conflicts where people live. What is the experience of those living near wind industry installations?
content.extendedDescription:
For people living in areas where wind power is planned, the impact starts long before any turbines are built. During project planning, many live with prolonged uncertainty: will the landscape change, will their home lose value, and how will nature and their living environment be affected? This uncertainty often creates significant psychological strain for those affected.

Once projects are built, everyday life changes noticeably. Large industrial turbines rise in formerly open landscapes, roads are built and natural environments are affected. For those living nearby, the sound of rotor blades can become a constant background presence, while flashing obstruction lights mark the installations in the night sky. For many, this creates a sense that a place once associated with home and recreation has fundamentally changed.

In this discussion, we want to highlight the human experiences behind wind power expansion – how decisions affect people living in the landscapes where projects are planned and built, and the consequences they experience.

content.title: How to build public-service buildings for greater wellbeing and a smaller climate footprint
content.description:

It is time to shift from the lowest construction cost to the best performance for wellbeing and low climate impact.
content.extendedDescription:

content.title: The mobile security chain – protecting critical data in public and private organisations
content.description: When patient data, trade secrets and other sensitive information are handled in everyday work, mobile phones become central to the risk landscape. How do we ensure appropriate protection without obstructing operations?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite advanced security solutions, many breaches occur through individual employees and human error. Mobile phones have become natural work tools in both public and private sectors and therefore central to organisations' overall risk exposure.
For organisations handling patient data, personal information and other sensitive material, this increases requirements for security design and monitoring. A mobile phone can be a vulnerable entry point but also an important part of the solution when managed properly.
Reducing risks requires a coordinated approach combining hardware, software, procedures and skills development, with regulatory requirements integrated into daily work. Cybersecurity must be treated as an operational issue with clear governance and long-term planning.
Samsung Norden invites you to an experience-based discussion of how organisations can work more systematically with mobile phones as part of their security efforts, focusing on concrete choices and sustainable solutions.

content.title: How can we build organisations that manage technological change and care for their people?
content.description: Tomorrow's organisations and society: what skills and leadership are needed to meet AI development, global uncertainty, rapid change and increasing demands? Many people feel stressed and threatened in their profession or expertise. How can Sweden remain competitive?
content.extendedDescription:

How can we build organisations that manage technological change while caring for the people experiencing it? How can we meet different generations' needs?

What will tomorrow's organisations need, and what do we need today? How should we design them?

content.title: Linguistic exclusion among deaf and hard-of-hearing children – what are the consequences?
content.description: Everyone talks about children's rights, but in practice those rights do not reach all children in Sweden. Sign language can counter loneliness and ill health, yet for the majority of the country's approximately 8,900 deaf and hard-of-hearing children, it is not a given part of life.
content.extendedDescription:
The report Dinner Table Syndrome and Existential Health – Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children's Experiences of Linguistic Exclusion, produced by Barn- och ungdomsjour på teckenspråk, deepens our understanding of what happens when children are not given the right to sign language and a language guarantee from day one.
The combination of research and in-depth interviews with support workers known as ‘syssnare’, who staff the world's only sign-language helpline for deaf and hard-of-hearing children and young people, clearly shows that this group needs support and empowerment to reduce its vulnerability and exposure to harm.

content.title: Support that safeguards legal rights for deaf and hard-of-hearing people with intellectual disabilities
content.description: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people with intellectual disabilities are a particularly vulnerable group who often miss out on support and assistance in sign language because of gaps in knowledge and accessibility. What happens when support and assistance fail to materialise? What is needed to provide help and support that safeguards their legal rights?
content.extendedDescription: People who are deaf or hard of hearing and also have a mild to moderate intellectual disability are a group about whom society knows very little. This is even more the case when they are victims of crime and different forms of violence. How well are this group's legal rights protected today? Sweden has 290 municipalities, all of which interpret, assess and provide support in different ways. Stöd på dina villkor is a project funded by Allmänna arvsfonden and run by Nationell kvinnojour och stöd på teckenspråk. The project began after several people with intellectual disabilities contacted the organisation's sign-language support line. Over three years, the project has collected, documented and developed methods for support work that can contribute to greater security and understanding for deaf and hard-of-hearing crime victims with intellectual disabilities. The discussion will explore these issues in greater depth through the project's work and present the results of its mapping of legal safeguards.

content.title: Never again war: the path from militarism to the development of civilisation
content.description: Blind faith in military solutions risks creating serious problems for future security and welfare. Rising military expenditure takes resources away from other important areas of society. How can we build a strong movement for peace and anti-militarism?
content.extendedDescription: The post-war cry of ‘Never again war!’ has turned into an ongoing war over resources, raw materials and territory. But war is a failure. Peace, by contrast, represents the development of human civilisation. It is time to abolish war and genuinely establish human security. We know there is no empirical evidence that war can produce stability and democracy. Blind faith in military solutions risks creating serious problems for the world's future security and welfare. Rising military expenditure takes resources away from other important areas of society. Roads, railways, schools, healthcare and elderly care face cuts while billions pour into new regiments. This is unsustainable and weakens preparedness for the problems we actually face, such as those related to the climate.

content.title: How the fight for Ojnareskogen became front-page news
content.description: What can we in Sápmi learn from the long struggle to protect Ojnareskogen and Lake Bästeträsk from industrial exploitation, and what can the special “Ojnare spirit” that developed during the process tell us about the power of civil society?
content.extendedDescription: The road towards the first national park on Gotland's main island has been long. Since Nordkalk applied to quarry limestone near Lake Bästeträsk more than 20 years ago, the struggle has involved legal proceedings, protests and strong local commitment. The planned Bästeträsk national park was due to open this summer, but parliament's decision has been delayed. Sofia Bothorp from Urbergsgruppen describes the battle for Ojnareskogen and the work behind the forthcoming national park.

content.title: Physical AI for industry – from pilot to production reality
content.description: Physical AI is moving from screens to machines, and Swedish industry faces a choice. How do we move from promising pilots to reliable production, and what is needed for Sweden to truly lead the industrial AI transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Circle Series is an initiative within Tech Forward, a collaboration between Techarenan and Teknikföretagen, bringing together 8–16 hand-picked decision-makers, experts and innovators to explore an urgent topic related to innovation, growth and the future in depth.

Unlike traditional panel discussions, Circle Series is an active conversation where everyone contributes. Each circle has a leader and meets 4–6 times over a year, creating continuity, trust and opportunities to move from insight to action.

The circle on physical AI for industry starts during Almedalsveckan 2026, meets again in the autumn and concludes at Techarenan's major event in February 2027.

content.title: Negative emissions today for a climate-neutral society
content.description: Negative emissions are necessary for society to become climate-neutral. So why is so little being done? Approved methods already exist that could be scaled up faster with support, while creating Swedish jobs. How slowly do we want progress to be?
content.extendedDescription:
The European Commission and the IPCC highlight biochar as a method for long-term carbon storage and negative emissions, and the Swedish inquiry into climate policy pathways (SOU 2020:4) identifies biochar as central to future negative emissions. Yet Sweden lacks a national strategy – unlike Denmark. What role do we want biochar to play in Sweden's climate transition, and how can we create governance that makes a difference?
The seminar brings together three perspectives: Meva Energy shows how biogenic residual streams can be used through gasification and the co-production of bioenergy and biochar. Waila examines biochar's properties and uses, including soil improvement. Lunds kommun describes how the public sector can drive development through procurement, strategic choices and local initiatives.
We conclude with an open discussion of the barriers, opportunities and requirements for scaling up the technology that already accounts for the largest amount of negative emissions in Sweden.

content.title: When words refuse to be silent: literature as resistance
content.description: Literature has the power to reveal what those in power want to hide. Through stories depicting oppression, war and injustice, authors can create spaces for truth, empathy and resistance.
content.extendedDescription: Literature becomes essential resistance when injustice and war silence people. Through words, authors can expose abuses of power, give a voice to those lost in violence and preserve experiences that might otherwise be erased. Stories offer the opportunity to understand, feel and question – and thus to create change. Literature defends human dignity, keeps memories alive and shows that another future is possible.
